newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist sees global flight within reach.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist sees global flight within reach.

text.p: Record-breaking U.S. adventurer Steve Fossett said on Tuesday that someone would fly around the world in a balloon within three years, but he declined to say if he would try his luck again.
After sailing halfway around the world, Fossett tackled his next challenge -- how to pull his tattered, $300,000 balloon from a tree in an Indian field.
One day after Fossett set down on the Ganges River plain, his "Solo Spirit" balloon still dangled from a "mahua" tree in a remote wheat field.

It took the 52-year-old commodity broker six days, two hours and 49 minutes to reach India after taking off from the U.S. heartland. He said he would now need some time before he could collect his gear and start home.

"I have a lot of things to do, packing up," Fossett told Reuters in Nonkhar village, some 550 km (330 miles) southeast of the Indian capital and more than 16,000 km (10,000 miles) from St Louis, Missouri, where he began his ascent on January 13.
"I need at least one more day here," he said.
Fossett told Reuters on Monday he believed his 45-metre (150-foot) balloon was ruined when it was shredded in the tree.
The day after Fossett broke a 16-year-old endurance record, the deflated balloon -- silver on the inside, off-white on the outside -- dangled in ribbons from the tree.

Silver propane cylinders lay in neat lines nearby. Microwave and very-high-frequency (VHF) antennae sprouted from the hatched, fibreglass vessel that had carried Fossett more than 16,000 km (10,000 miles) over the Atlantic and North Africa.
On the side was written "Steve Fossett" in large letters.
A police cordon kept curious villagers from approaching the balloon. Fossett's support team said it was unclear how the "Solo Spirit" would be extracted from the mahua tree's broken branches.
Villagers said the fermented mahua fruit was used to make a local liquor.
"We could have given him a mahua drink, but he asked for milk instead," said Hanuman Singh, a farmer who was among those to greet Fossett after he descended to earth on Monday.
Fossett said he was happy to have broken two ballooning records -- the greatest distance and longest time in the air -- before running short of fuel, and he called his aborted mission a success.
"There are a number of competing teams to try and make it around the world and I think one of them will succeed within three years," Fossett said.

"My team has the most experience with this kind of flight. We certainly have a good chance of being the first person to do it," he told Reuters earlier outside a government guest house in nearby Sultanpur where he spent the night.
But he declined to say whether he himself would make a fresh bid. "I just have to reflect," he said.
Fossett said it took him hours on Monday before he found a telephone with which he could call overseas, and that he had talked to his wife in the United States.
"She was very, very happy. She was relieved that I didn't fall into the Atlantic," he said.
He said he was in for a surprise when he had his first copious meal on Monday night. "They gave me a Chinese meal. I was expecting them to bring some Indian food," he said.
Clean-shaven and dressed in a yellow pullover and grey trousers, Fossett said he was looking forward to some more rest.
"I would love to have a vacation now," he said. "That's a very good idea. Have a cocktail and watch television."
